lair-of-the-white-worm:
Bram Stoker wrote this last novel of his life, and it came out in 1911, a year before his death. He set it in his wife's home shire, in the north of England. The tale draws on a local legend of a great white worm that plagued the land.

A young man comes home to find a strange, cold feud round two old houses. Lady Arabella, one of the foes, hides a dread link to the worm of the old tale. Weird and hot with dread, the book is the most strange of all Stoker's works.
ostrovsky-the-storm:
Katerina, trapped in a loveless marriage under a tyrannical mother-in-law, reaches for love and is destroyed in Ostrovsky's The Storm, in English. A thunderstorm breaks over her Volga town as her inner tempest breaks into confession. The play, from 1859, became Russia's great tragedy of a woman's revolt against the dark kingdom of merchant patriarchy.

Katerina's longing for freedom is phrased like prayer and poetry, set against the Kabanovs' airless household. Her lover is too weak, her world too strong, and the river waits below the cliff. The drama inspired Janacek's opera Katya Kabanova, carrying her story across Europe. Russian audiences have wept over Katerina for over a century and a half. The Storm remains Ostrovsky's summit.
